description:
Before the war the Soviets had begun digging pits in a wooded area near Paneriai station, on the edge of Vilnius, to hold fuel storage tanks. The work was unfinished when German forces arrived in June 1941. The pits were used instead as execution sites and mass graves.

Shooting began in July 1941 and continued until August 1944. The killing was carried out by German SD and Security Police units together with the Ypatingasis burys, a Lithuanian special squad of around eighty men. Most victims were Jews from Vilnius and the surrounding towns, walked or driven the few kilometres out from the ghetto. Polish civilians, including members of the intelligentsia, and Soviet prisoners of war were also shot there.

By the end of 1941 the great majority of Vilnius Jews were already dead. The ghetto was liquidated in 1943 and the remaining population sent to camps or shot at the pits.

Kazimierz Sakowicz, a Polish journalist living beside the site, watched from his attic and kept a dated record of what he saw, burying the pages in bottles. He was shot in July 1944. His diary was recovered after the war and is one of the few contemporaneous accounts of a mass shooting site written by a bystander.

description:
Treblinka II was the third killing centre of Operation Reinhard, after Belzec and Sobibor. It was built in the summer of 1942 in a forest about 80 kilometres northeast of Warsaw, on a rail spur off the Warsaw to Bialystok line, and began operating on 23 July 1942. A separate forced labour camp, Treblinka I, had been running nearby since late 1941, its prisoners worked mainly in a gravel pit.

The camp had no other purpose. Transports arrived by rail and almost everyone on them was gassed within hours. A small number of Jewish men were held back as a Sonderkommando and forced to empty the chambers and bury the dead. Three commandants ran it in sixteen months: Irmfried Eberl, then Franz Stangl, then Kurt Franz.

In 1943 the SS had the mass graves reopened and the bodies burned on open pyres to destroy the evidence. On 2 August 1943 the Sonderkommando revolted, set part of the camp alight and several hundred prisoners broke out. Most were hunted down. Gassing ended that October and the camp was levelled, planted over and disguised as a farm.

Treblinka I kept running until July 1944, when the SS shot the prisoners still there as the Red Army approached. Soviet troops reached both sites in the last week of that month.
notes: Hofle telegram figure of 713555 double-counts against EV0133 and any Operation Reinhard parent record. Reconcile before both publish.

description:
German Army Group North closed the last land route into Leningrad on 8 September 1941. The city was not taken by assault and was not meant to be. German planning treated starving the population as the method, with Leningrad to be razed afterwards, and an order forbade feeding anyone who came out.

A Luftwaffe raid on the day the ring closed destroyed a large part of the city's food stores. Rations fell through the autumn until, at the worst point, a worker received 250 grams of bread a day and children, the elderly and the unemployed received 125 grams. The winter of 1941 to 1942 was exceptionally cold, with temperatures below minus 40 Celsius, and it killed the most people. Around 2,000 people were arrested for cannibalism in the first half of 1942.

Supplies came in over the ice of Lake Ladoga, a route known as the Road of Life, and evacuations went out the same way. It was never enough to feed the city, but it kept it alive.

The blockade lasted 872 days and was lifted on 27 January 1944. A prewar population of over three million had fallen to roughly 750,000 by late summer 1942.

description:
The Ustase regime of the Independent State of Croatia set up the Jasenovac complex in August 1941 on the banks of the Sava, about 100 kilometres southeast of Zagreb. Unlike almost every other camp system in occupied Europe it was not run by the Germans. Department III of the Ustase Supervisory Service ran it, under Vjekoslav Luburic.

It was never one camp. The first two, Krapje and Brocica, opened in August 1941 and closed four months later. Three more followed and ran until the end: Ciglana, a brickworks; Kozara, a tannery; and Stara Gradiska, an old Austro-Hungarian fortress converted into a camp for women and children in the winter of 1942. Around them were five work farms, a Roma camp at Ustica, and the killing grounds at Donja Gradina across the river, which sit in Bosnia today while the rest of the site is in Croatia.

Prisoners were Serbs, Roma, Jews, and Croats and Bosnian Muslims who opposed the regime. Some were shot at Gradina and Granik, some were worked or starved to death, and many were killed by hand. Jews with useful trades were kept alive; in 1942 and 1943 most of the survivors were handed to the Germans for Auschwitz.

The Ustase razed the camp in April 1945 as the Partisans approached, burning the buildings and the records with them.

description:
The Japanese Central China Area Army took Nanjing, then the capital of the Republic of China, on 13 December 1937. What followed lasted roughly six weeks, and atrocities in the wider Nanjing area ran from early December 1937 into March 1938.

Captured Chinese soldiers were executed in large numbers in violation of the laws of war, along with male civilians identified as soldiers on no evidence beyond their age. Groups were taken to the banks of the Yangtze and to open ground outside the walls and shot, bayoneted or machine gunned. Arson destroyed about a third of the city, and the killing extended well past the walls into the surrounding counties.

A small group of foreign residents established a Safety Zone and sheltered around 250,000 civilians across 25 refugee camps. Their records, along with burial counts kept by the Red Swastika Society and the Chongshantang, became central evidence afterwards, and the reliability of those burial counts is still argued over.

The International Military Tribunal for the Far East tried the case at Tokyo between 1946 and 1948, and a separate Nanjing War Crimes Tribunal sat in China. Both reached findings on the scale of the killing, and those findings do not agree with each other. Mass sexual violence ran alongside the killing throughout and is recorded separately as EV0376.

In December 1981 the Salvadoran army carried out a counterinsurgency sweep through northern Morazan, in territory held by the FMLN. The Atlacatl Battalion led it. The Tutela Legal report also identifies the Salvadoran Air Force, the Artillery Brigade, the Third Infantry Brigade of San Miguel and the Commando Instruction Centre at San Francisco Gotera.

The killing was not confined to El Mozote. It ran through the hamlets and cantons around it: La Joya, Cerro Pando, Jocote Amarillo, Rancheria and Los Toriles. Tutela Legal later identified 765 victims by name, a large proportion of them children.

The government denied it had happened and the denial held for a decade. In 1992 the United Nations Truth Commission ordered exhumations, carried out by an Argentine forensic team. One pit held the remains of 133 children. The Commission reported in March 1993. An amnesty law was passed five days later and closed the case.

El Salvador's Supreme Court struck that amnesty down in 2016. The criminal investigation reopened at San Francisco Gotera, with seventeen former officers charged, and survivors gave evidence in court for the first time.

description:
Union Carbide India Limited ran a pesticide plant at Bhopal producing Sevin, which required methyl isocyanate as an intermediate. The gas was stored on site in bulk tanks. On the night of 2 to 3 December 1984, water entered tank E610, and the resulting runaway reaction released around 45 tonnes of methyl isocyanate into the air.

The gas is heavier than air. It settled over the densely populated neighbourhoods immediately around the plant and spread through the city while people slept. More than half a million people were exposed. Those who woke and ran generally survived; those who did not, or who ran the wrong way, often did not.

A 2006 government affidavit put the injuries at 558,125, including 38,478 temporary partial injuries and around 3,900 cases of severe permanent disability. Survivors continued to die of respiratory, neurological and other gas related illness for decades.

The site was never properly cleaned. Hundreds of tonnes of waste remained, soil and groundwater were contaminated, and in 2004 the Indian Supreme Court ordered the state to supply clean drinking water to residents. In 2010 a Bhopal court convicted seven former UCIL executives, all Indian nationals, of negligence.

description:
By early 1945 the American high altitude precision bombing of Japan had achieved little. Major General Curtis LeMay, commanding XXI Bomber Command from the Marianas, changed the method: B-29s would come in at night, at low altitude, stripped of most defensive guns, carrying incendiaries instead of high explosive.

The target on the night of 9 to 10 March 1945 was the shitamachi, the dense working class districts of eastern Tokyo around Koto and Chuo, built largely of wood and paper. Pathfinders marked the area with a burning X. Around 280 aircraft then dropped roughly 1,665 tonnes of incendiaries, mostly M-69 bomblets that scattered jets of burning napalm.

The fires merged. Winds of nearly 30 miles an hour carried the firestorm through the districts faster than people could run from it. Canals and rivers filled with those who tried to shelter in the water. Around 16 square miles of the city burned out in a single night and about a million people were left homeless.

The raid killed more people than either atomic bombing. Survivors received no state compensation, and in 2007 bereaved families brought a class action against the Japanese government seeking an apology and damages.

description:
When Nanjing fell on 13 December 1937, Japanese soldiers began raping women and girls throughout the city: in houses, in the street, and inside the refugee camps meant to be shelter. Victims ranged from children to elderly women. Many were raped by groups of soldiers, many were killed afterwards, and relatives who tried to intervene were shot.

The International Military Tribunal for the Far East found that roughly 20,000 rapes were committed inside the city in the first month of the occupation. Later scholarship generally gives a range of 20,000 to 80,000. Neither is a count. Both are bounded by what a small number of foreign witnesses could see and by how little survivors could safely report.

Ginling College, the women's college inside the Safety Zone, was run through the occupation by the American missionary Minnie Vautrin with her Chinese colleague Tsen Shui-fang. It held about 10,000 women and children. Soldiers came to the gates repeatedly to take women out, and the two women spent weeks turning them away.

The documentary record has a gap in it that matters. When the International Committee for the Nanking Safety Zone submitted its 60 page report in June 1938, sexual violence was left out of it. The material reached the Tokyo tribunal by other routes and was accepted there. Most of the surviving first hand accounts sit in the missionary papers of John Magee, Robert Wilson, Lewis Smythe and Vautrin, held at Yale Divinity School Library.

description:
This is one of the forced labour camps run in and around Moscow between 1919 and 1922, in the period the Soviet camp system was being invented rather than administered.

Concentration camps became official policy in the RSFSR with the Council of People's Commissars decree on the Red Terror, and the camps themselves were created by a decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee that came into force on 15 April 1919, with a further decree of 17 May 1919 putting them under a Department of Forced Labour. They served two purposes at once. They held prisoners of the Civil War, and they frightened everybody else. Among the first people in them were hostages: relatives of men who had joined the White armies, residents of front-line districts, people whose only qualification was who they were related to or where they lived.

In Moscow the buildings used were mostly monasteries and convents, emptied and repurposed. That is why so many of these records sit on religious foundations. The camps were run locally, with local work, and had no economic plan behind them yet; that came later, with Solovki and then the Gulag proper. Many of them simply failed and shut. An enactment of 1922 left the GPU only two places of confinement in the whole country, one in Moscow and one in Petrograd, and transferred some three hundred Cheka camps and prisons to the NKVD.

What is established about this particular site is thin. Memorial places it as recorded below, and the scholarship on the Moscow Governorate camps works from camp activity reports, inspection files and prisoner statistics held in the archives. Nobody has opened those for this record.
notes: 2-ya Moskovskaya tyuremnaya bolnitsa

description:
This is one of the forced labour camps run in and around Moscow between 1919 and 1922, in the period the Soviet camp system was being invented rather than administered.

Concentration camps became official policy in the RSFSR with the Council of People's Commissars decree on the Red Terror, and the camps themselves were created by a decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee that came into force on 15 April 1919, with a further decree of 17 May 1919 putting them under a Department of Forced Labour. They served two purposes at once. They held prisoners of the Civil War, and they frightened everybody else. Among the first people in them were hostages: relatives of men who had joined the White armies, residents of front-line districts, people whose only qualification was who they were related to or where they lived.

In Moscow the buildings used were mostly monasteries and convents, emptied and repurposed. That is why so many of these records sit on religious foundations. The camps were run locally, with local work, and had no economic plan behind them yet; that came later, with Solovki and then the Gulag proper. Many of them simply failed and shut. An enactment of 1922 left the GPU only two places of confinement in the whole country, one in Moscow and one in Petrograd, and transferred some three hundred Cheka camps and prisons to the NKVD.

What is established about this particular site is thin. Memorial places it as recorded below, and the scholarship on the Moscow Governorate camps works from camp activity reports, inspection files and prisoner statistics held in the archives. Nobody has opened those for this record.

description:
Number 11 Varsonofevsky Lane is a courtyard building about three hundred metres from Lubyanka Square. It was the execution garage.

People held in the Lubyanka inner prison were brought here to be shot. It worked as the step between the investigation and the grave, and Muscovites knew enough to avoid the lane: rumours about what happened in the yard were already circulating during the Civil War. Vasily Blokhin, the Lubyanka commandant, ran executions here from 1926 until 1953.

Marshal Tukhachevsky was shot here, with the prosecutor Vyshinsky and Ulrikh of the Military Collegium present. So was Yezhov, the NKVD chief who had built much of the machine, killed by Blokhin, who had worked for him.

The building is still there. The only commemorative plaque on it records that Dzerzhinsky once worked in the building. Nothing on it says what the yard was used for.

description:
Butyrka is the oldest of the three Moscow prisons that mattered in the terror. The present building went up in 1879, on the site of a fortress-like prison built under Catherine the Great to a design by Matvei Kazakov. It had held political prisoners long before the Bolsheviks: hundreds of participants in the Polish January Uprising of 1863 were kept in its towers.

Under the Soviets it served mainly as the prison people were moved to after interrogation, while they waited for transport to the camps. That made it the last Moscow address for a very large number of people, and it was crowded and filthy for most of its Soviet history.

Memorial records it as a place of execution as well as detention. Prisoners were also taken from here to Butovo to be shot.

It is still in use. Butyrka is now a pre-trial detention centre run by the Federal Penitentiary Service and remains the largest remand prison in Moscow, with overcrowding an ongoing problem.

description:
This is one of the prisons of Moscow that Memorial records as part of the apparatus of political repression.

The system had a shape. People were arrested and taken first to a district arrest house or straight to an investigation prison, of which the inner prison at the Lubyanka was the most important. Interrogation happened there. Once a case was closed, prisoners were moved to a holding prison such as Butyrka or a transit prison such as Krasnaya Presnya to wait for a sentence to be carried out or for transport to a camp. Those sentenced to death were taken to be shot elsewhere, and their bodies to a cemetery or crematorium that had been told to expect them.

Each of these buildings did one job in that sequence, and which job it did says more about what happened to a person inside it than the building's own history does.

Specific detail on this prison has not been established for this record. Memorial's entry is the only source and its page has not been opened.

description:
Butovo was an estate south of Moscow seized after the 1917 revolution and held by the OGPU, then the NKVD, which used it as an agricultural colony and a firing range. In 1937 it was turned into an execution and burial ground.

The first 91 victims arrived from Moscow prisons on 8 August 1937. City cemeteries could not absorb the numbers the Great Terror was producing, so the NKVD designated Butovo and Kommunarka to take them. Prisoners were brought at night, largely from the Taganskaya, Butyrskaya and Sretenskaya prisons, shot, and buried in long trenches dug by excavator. The heaviest single day was 28 February 1938, when 562 people were shot.

Unlike Kommunarka, which took the Soviet elite, Butovo received ordinary people: workers, peasants, clergy, office staff, non-party members, and people of many nationalities. Sixty-nine of the dead were juveniles. The youngest was Mikhail Shamonin, aged thirteen.

The ground stayed inside the security services until 1995, fenced and guarded, and was then transferred to the Russian Orthodox Church. Thirteen mass graves have been identified. One caution carried by the Iofe Foundation's necropolis project: whether the shooting itself happened at Butovo rests on statements by former NKVD staff and is not established by document. The burials are documented. Say which is which.

description:
Kommunarka was a state farm and the dacha of NKVD chief Genrikh Yagoda, about 8 km northwest of Butovo. After Yagoda's own arrest the NKVD turned it into a burial ground, designated a special site.

Burials began on 21 October 1937 and ran systematically until mid-1938, resumed in 1939, and are assumed to have restarted when war broke out in 1941. Bodies were placed in trenches prepared in advance. Where Butovo took ordinary people, Kommunarka took the Soviet elite: party officials, military commanders, diplomats and administrators swept up in the case of the Right-Trotskyist bloc and what followed it.

Excavation has confirmed 47 pits, between 5 and 15 metres long and 2 to 5 metres wide. The eastern and southern parts of the site appear not to have been used for mass burial.

As at Butovo, former NKVD staff and local residents described executions taking place on site when asked in the late 1980s and early 1990s, but that has not been documented. What is documented is the burial.

The 2018 survey by the State Museum of the History of the Gulag, led by the archaeologist Mikhail Zhukovsky with Anatoly Kantarovich of Moscow University, worked from Luftwaffe aerial reconnaissance photographs taken on 26 August 1942 and read them with computer photogrammetry, then cut stratigraphic sections on the ground. That is how the 47 pits were found, in the western corner of the site above the Ordynka. It established where the burials are. It did not establish who is in them.

description:
Between 1926 and 1935 the bodies of people sentenced to be shot by the OGPU and NKVD, together with people who died in Moscow's prisons, were buried secretly at Vagankovskoe. It is a large public cemetery, founded in 1771 and holding more than a hundred thousand graves, and that was the point: the dead were hidden among the ordinary dead of the city.

What establishes it is paperwork. Documents in the investigation files held by the FSB central archive and the FSB departments for Moscow and the Moscow Region record the burials. Correspondence between the organisations that carried out executions and those that ran the city's cemeteries and crematoria is, in Memorial's assessment, the only reliable official source for where Moscow's mass graves are.

The cemetery itself has never been investigated. The number of people secretly buried here is not established and may never be.

In 1995 Memorial published a first list of 733 names, since enlarged. A memorial was placed by the entrance in 1994, reading: to the victims of political repression, 1927 to 1937.

From 1935 until the early 1950s the bodies of people shot in Moscow prisons were taken to the crematorium at the former Donskoe Monastery and burned. This was disposal, not burial. The site's function in the terror was to make the dead unfindable.

The ashes went into common pits beside the crematorium, recorded in the cemetery's own paperwork under the phrase burials of uncollected ashes. Three of these lie in the northern part of the graveyard. Common Grave No. 1 is dated 1932 to 1940, No. 2 covers 1943 to 1944, and No. 3 runs from 1945 to 1989. Some bodies were also interred rather than cremated, mainly in 1937.

Nobody knows who is in which pit. The dead were mixed by the method, and that was the point of it.

A granite plaque went up on Common Grave No. 1 in August 1991 and a pillar on No. 3 in 1994. Collective and personal memorials have accumulated around them since. The graveyard is open daily and holds local protected status.

description:
The cemetery of the Yauza Hospital was the first of Moscow's secret burial grounds for the executed. Between 1921 and 1926 the bodies of people shot on political charges were buried on the hospital's territory. The hospital still stands and is now City Hospital No. 23.

Moscow's disposal of its dead moved as the numbers grew. Yauza took them until 1926, Vagankovskoe cemetery from 1926 to 1935, then the Donskoe crematorium from 1934 into the 1950s, and from 1936 and 1937 the two NKVD special sites outside the city, Butovo and Kommunarka. Each of those is a separate record in this file.

Memorial's plaque outside the Lubyanka names this chain. It states that more than forty thousand people were shot in Moscow on groundless political charges, and lists where they were put.

What is not known is how many of them are here.

description:
Lefortovo was built in 1881 and became the NKVD's interrogation prison in Moscow. It is built as a letter K, and the memoirist Dmitri Panin, who was held there, described a warder standing at the centre of the three wings directing the movement of prisoners to and from interrogation with a flag, so that no two prisoners would meet.

The building's whole design is about that separation. It was not a transit prison and not a camp. It was where confessions were produced.

By the late 1930s it was so overcrowded that the NKVD opened an annex outside the city, in the Sukhanovsky monastery, which became Special Object No. 110 and acquired a worse reputation than the parent prison.

Lefortovo is still operational and has been under the Ministry of Justice since 2005.

description:
Sukhanovka was opened in 1938, on Yezhov's order, inside the buildings of the former Ekaterininskaya Pustyn monastery near Vidnoye, south of Moscow. Its official name was Special Object No. 110. It appears in no public list of prisons, and prisoners were not told where they were.

It existed because Lefortovo had run out of room. What it became was something else: the place the NKVD sent people it intended to break rather than merely hold. Monastic cells were used for solitary confinement. Survivors described sleep deprivation, cells too small to sit down in, rooms deliberately overheated or left freezing, and no exercise outdoors. Beria kept an office on the site and attended interrogations himself.

Prisoners who had been through several Moscow prisons rated this one the worst. One survivor, moved on to Butyrka afterwards, described Butyrka as feeling like a holiday camp by comparison.

Yezhov was held here from 10 April 1939, after his own fall. He was tried in the prison governor's office in February 1940 and shot in Moscow, in the execution yard on Varsonofevsky Lane. The site later became a women's prison, then a police training school. It is a working monastery again, and the community there now cares for the Kommunarka burial ground.
notes: Sukhanovskaya osoborezhimnaya tyurma Cross-references: Yezhov was executed at the Varsonofevsky Lane yard, which is a separate record in this file. The St Catherine monastery community on this site now cares for the Kommunarka burial ground, also a separate record.

description:
This is one of the prisons of Moscow that Memorial records as part of the apparatus of political repression.

The system had a shape. People were arrested and taken first to a district arrest house or straight to an investigation prison, of which the inner prison at the Lubyanka was the most important. Interrogation happened there. Once a case was closed, prisoners were moved to a holding prison such as Butyrka or a transit prison such as Krasnaya Presnya to wait for a sentence to be carried out or for transport to a camp. Those sentenced to death were taken to be shot elsewhere, and their bodies to a cemetery or crematorium that had been told to expect them.

Each of these buildings did one job in that sequence, and which job it did says more about what happened to a person inside it than the building's own history does.

description:
This is one of the NKVD's special technical bureaus, known in prison slang as a sharashka: a design office staffed by prisoners.

The pattern began in 1930, when Leonid Ramzin and other engineers convicted in the Industrial Party trial were put to work as a design bureau under the OGPU rather than sent to camps. It was formalised on 29 September 1938 as the Department of Special Design Bureaus of the NKVD, renamed the Special Technical Bureau in January 1939 under General Valentin Kravchenko and Beria's direct supervision, and given the cover name 4th Special Department in 1941. It ran until 1953.

Conditions were better than a camp. There were beds, showers, libraries, no felling timber in the snow. That is the part usually told, and it is true, and it is also the reason these places are easy to misread. The men working here were prisoners. They had been arrested on fabricated charges, several of them sentenced to death first, and they were designing aircraft, engines and weapons under armed guard to earn their way out. Their results were commonly published under the names of scientists who were not in prison, and the real authors went uncredited.

Specific detail on this bureau is thin. Memorial places it as recorded below. The numbered OTB and OKB units are documented in Russian archival scholarship that has not been opened for this record.

description:
The inner prison at Bolshaya Lubyanka was the investigation prison of the Cheka and its successors. People arrested in political cases were brought here, interrogated here, and held here while their case was assembled.

It was small. It was never a camp and never a transit prison. Its function was to produce the confession on which a sentence would rest.

One thing worth stating plainly, because the opposite is widely believed: current research indicates that nobody was executed at Lubyanka. The building was the central administration of the security service, its investigation offices and this prison. The shooting was done elsewhere, most of it a few minutes' walk away at the yard on Varsonofevsky Lane.

That matters for a map. Lubyanka Square has absorbed almost all of the public memory of the terror in Moscow, while the places where people were actually killed and buried sit outside it, unmarked and largely unvisited.

description:
This is one of the prisons of Moscow that Memorial records as part of the apparatus of political repression.

The system had a shape. People were arrested and taken first to a district arrest house or straight to an investigation prison, of which the inner prison at the Lubyanka was the most important. Interrogation happened there. Once a case was closed, prisoners were moved to a holding prison such as Butyrka or a transit prison such as Krasnaya Presnya to wait for a sentence to be carried out or for transport to a camp. Those sentenced to death were taken to be shot elsewhere, and their bodies to a cemetery or crematorium that had been told to expect them.

Each of these buildings did one job in that sequence, and which job it did says more about what happened to a person inside it than the building's own history does.
